Science Background:
Combustion of solid fuels in microgravity has been an active area of research
Numerical models predict that 1-g buoyant flows profoundly affect fuel flammability
Microgravity experiments burning thin fuels have verified this prediction, but ground-based facilities are too short to examine the burning of thicker fuels

Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Hypotheses
:
Materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, may burn more readily compared to normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.)   
As a result, the 1-g test currently used by NASA to rate materials for space may need to be re-evaluated from a margin-of-safety point of view.
Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Objective:
Bridge the gap between normal gravity, NASA-STD-6001 Test # 1 method, ground based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
Material selection for spacecraft is based on 1-g tests
Model and drop tower results suggest 1-g may not represent the most flammable condition in some cases
Long duration tests will refine test criteria and modeling efforts
Test the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, and flow.
Local extinguishment of flame has some advantages
Geometry and flow can affect optimal suppression delivery

Why ISS for BASS?
Relationship 
between ground test and microgravity test can be determined by observing flames burning for longer times.
Practical, realistic fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object.
Models can be validated and developed.
Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Science Applications 
for Space
: 
The microgravity burning 
and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples 
will be determined.  
The 
current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.  These results will suggest 
improved strategies by linking actual long-duration burn behavior in microgravity to Earth-based selection methods.
Guidance for strategies to extinguish 
accidental fires in 
microgravity will be provided.  
Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Science Applications 
for Earth
: 
 
BASS results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.  
Detailed 
combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity.  Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity.  These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems.
Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Differences from SLICE:
Solid fuel samples burned (instead of gaseous jets)
All but the flat samples will be burned multiple times
The nozzle is used to deliver nitrogen (for extinguishment) in some cases
The igniter typically needs to be positioned manually prior to the test
Within 1 mm of fuel (but not touching fuel) when in position 
Out of flame zone and camera fields of view when retracted
Immediately after ignition: don’t touch window when retracted, or hold away to cool for first ~ 10 s or it may stick to plastic door or break
Burning And Suppression of Solids (BASS)

Differences from SLICE (
con’t
):
Flow: Control box is different
Allows potentiometer to go all the way to zero so the flow may be shut off gradually 
There is some fan hysteresis because the fan must start from a stopped position and thus overcome static coefficient of friction and resistance
Nozzle flow is labeled “GN2” instead of “Fuel” (but note that screen display will still indicate “Fuel”)
Fan calibration to be performed with 0, 1, and 2 screens; we will likely use mostly one of these configurations based on the calibration results
Wax sample tests will be done last to minimize possible flow system blockage by wax re-condensation on downstream flow system
